prompt:
TASK: READ ONE INSTRUMENT ENTRY AND ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS

Below is one entry from the specification of a web measurement instrument. The instrument checks
public websites of U.S. federal statistical agencies and reports, per agency, whether each check
passed or failed. The entry states the check's question, the behavior a ready publisher is
expected to show (with verbatim quotes from the sources it cites), the test the instrument runs,
and what a pass and a fail claim.

Terms the project defines once for every entry (they are not undefined): SI client (SI system): a system that finds, reads and uses data on its own, such as an answer engine, an agent or a retrieval pipeline; the project's term for what is elsewhere called an AI system; data page: an agency's own web page for one data product, the page the harness measures (also 'product page' in rule code); harness: this project's scanner: an identified, robots-compliant HTTP client that fetches the pages and records what it met; cycle of record: the scan whose results the published grid is built from (here scan_2026-10-07_composite_d); recorded location: an address for an agency's API, terms, changelog or inventory that the harness was given, read from the agency's own pages or seeded from a named source; error / not measured: the harness could not observe: an access denial, its own robots compliance, an absence it could not confirm, or a server or network error; never a fail

Answer from the entry alone. For question 1, the QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES are the only evidence of
what the sources say; do not use what you know of them from elsewhere.

1. Does the EXPECTED BEHAVIOR come from the cited sources and not from the writer? Answer "yes"
   if every requirement the expected-behavior text attributes to a source is supported by a
   quoted passage, and any part no source defines is said plainly to be undefined or the
   project's own. Answer "no" if it states as a source's requirement something the passages do
   not contain; name it.
2. Could a reader who knows the agency misread a FAIL on this check as a claim the test did not
   make? Answer "yes" if the CLAIMS leave such a misreading open (name it), "no" if they close it.
3. Is any term in the entry undefined for a technically literate reader new to this project?
   Answer "yes" and list the terms, or "no".

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"q1": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q2": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "terms": ["..."], "why": "..."}}

ENTRY
CHECK: A5 (RULE-A5-v2)

QUESTION:
Is the data page listed in the host's sitemap? Search engines and answer engines discover pages by following links and reading sitemaps; on a large site, a page a sitemap omits can go undiscovered, and an SI client cannot cite a page its retrieval layer never found.
Established by: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4: agencies should employ best practices to improve crawling or indexing of web content, including using sitemaps); sitemaps-protocol (Sitemaps are a way for webmasters to inform search engines about pages on their sites that are available for crawling)

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR:
Federal agencies should use sitemaps to improve crawling and indexing (M-23-22 §III.4). The sitemaps protocol defines the file, its scope (a sitemap lists URLs at and below its own location, on one host) and its declaration in robots.txt. Google states that a large site benefits from a sitemap that lists the pages the owner wants found, and that a small, comprehensively linked site may not need one.
Cited sources: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4); sitemaps-protocol (Sitemap file location; Specifying the Sitemap location in your robots.txt file); https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview (Do I need a sitemap?)

QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES (verbatim):
- [omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience] "Agencies should employ best practices to improve crawling or indexing of web content, including using sitemaps, robots.txt files"
- [sitemaps-protocol] "The location of a Sitemap file determines the set of URLs that can be included in that Sitemap."
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "You might not need a sitemap if"
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "in most cases, your site will benefit from having a sitemap"

TEST:
Client: the harness's identified, robots-compliant client
Request: GET /sitemap.xml, /sitemap_index.xml, the sitemap(s) robots.txt declares (same site only), /llms.txt and /.well-known/ discovery paths; parse sitemaps with ultimate-sitemap-parser
Reads: whether any served sitemap lists the data page's URL
Decision rule:
- pass: `sitemap at {url} lists the product URL`
- fail: `discovery files served ({urls}) but none lists the product URL`
- fail: `no sitemap, llms.txt or well-known discovery file served`
- not_applicable: the host declares a sitemap on another site, which the harness records and does not fetch
Parameters: a URL matches when it equals the data page's URL as the frame records it
Is it the recognized way to measure the behavior: Reading the sitemap and looking for the URL is what a crawler does with it (sitemaps protocol). No published method defines a pass/fail for "the page is listed"; the harness's rule (listed or not) is the direct reading.

BRANCHES (each verdict branch of the rule; the behavior it rewards or penalizes; its source):
- pass_listed_in_sitemap (pass): a sitemap served on the host lists the data page Source: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4); sitemaps-protocol (protocol).
- fail_served_but_not_listed (fail): the host serves a sitemap or llms.txt that does not list the data page Source: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4); https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview (Do I need a sitemap?).
- fail_no_discovery_file (fail): the host serves no sitemap at the probed locations Source: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4).

CLAIMS:
A pass claims: A sitemap served on the agency's host lists this data page's address.
A fail claims: The host's sitemaps (and any llms.txt) were read and none lists this data page's address, or no sitemap is served at the standard locations. It is not a claim that search engines cannot find the page: well-linked pages are found without a sitemap.
Neither claims: Nothing about whether the page is indexed by any engine, or about sitemaps on other hosts.

CONFOUNDS:
- the sitemap lists the page under a different URL form (trailing slash, redirect target, query string). Distinguished: no: a fail.
- the only discovery file served is llms.txt, which by its proposal summarises a site rather than listing every page. Distinguished: no: the served-but-not-listed branch does not separate llms.txt from a sitemap in its verdict, only in its reason's URLs.
- the sitemap is declared on another site. Distinguished: yes: not_applicable.
response_text: {"q1": {"answer": "no", "why": "Two attributions outrun the quoted passages. (a) The entry says the sitemaps protocol defines the sitemap's 'declaration in robots.txt' and its scope as 'on one host'; the only sitemaps-protocol quote is 'The location of a Sitemap file determines the set of URLs that can be included in that Sitemap', which supports a location-bound scope but says nothing about robots.txt declaration or a single-host limit (the robots.txt section is named in 'Cited sources' but never quoted). (b) The entry says Google 'states that a large site benefits from a sitemap that lists the pages the owner wants found, and that a small, comprehensively linked site may not need one'; the Google quotes are only the truncated 'You might not need a sitemap if' and 'in most cases, your site will benefit from having a sitemap', which contain no large/small-site conditions, no 'comprehensively linked' condition, and nothing about listing the pages the owner wants found. The M-23-22 attribution is supported. The entry does not mark the unsupported parts as the project's own."}, "q2": {"answer": "yes", "why": "The fail claim says 'none lists this data page's address', but the Parameters restrict a match to exact equality with the URL 'as the frame records it', and the Confounds admit that a sitemap listing the page under a trailing slash, redirect target or query-string variant is scored as a fail. A reader who knows the agency's sitemap does list the page (in a variant form) would read the fail as a claim that the page is absent from the sitemap, a claim the test does not make; the Claims section never states the exact-string condition. A second opening: the served-but-not-listed branch fires when only llms.txt is served, so a reader could take a fail as 'the agency's sitemap omits the page' when the agency serves no sitemap at all and llms.txt by design does not enumerate pages; the Claims text ('The host's sitemaps (and any llms.txt) were read') does not separate these cases."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes", "terms": ["frame (\"as the frame records it\")", "llms.txt", "/.well-known/ discovery paths (which paths)", "reason / \"its reason's URLs\"", "ultimate-sitemap-parser"], "why": "'Frame' is used as the authority for the data page's canonical URL but is defined nowhere in the entry or the project glossary given. 'llms.txt' is referred to by 'its proposal' without saying what it is or whose proposal. The test requests '/.well-known/ discovery paths' without naming which well-known paths are probed, so the reader cannot tell what counts as a served discovery file. 'Reason' (in 'only in its reason's URLs') refers to an output field of the verdict that the entry never introduces. 'ultimate-sitemap-parser' is named as the parser with no indication that it is a third-party library or how it treats sitemap indexes, which bears on what 'any served sitemap' covers."}}
